newsitem.title: USA: New data shows U.S. expansion to continue.
newsitem.headline: New data shows U.S. expansion to continue.

text.p: The 6-year-old economic expansion seems poised to continue pressing ahead well into next year, according to data reported Monday.
The Conference Board's Index of Leading Indicators inched higher in November after holding steady in October, the private research group said.
The index, designed to forecast economic trends six to nine months down the road, rose 0.1 percent in November after being unchanged in October and rising 0.1 percent in September.

At the same time, the National Association of Realtors reported a respectable 1.8 percent rise in the sales of existing homes last month to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 4.04 million. Compared with a year ago, the resale pace was up 1 percent.
The new data seemed to suggest that the economy, while hardly setting off fireworks, still had enough steam to keep the protracted expansion from cooling down, analysts said.
"What we are seeing is just more of the same," said economist David Wyss of DRI/McGraw-Hill Inc.
He predicted the economy will move ahead by 2 percent to 2.5 percent next year, a little softer in the beginning, then gaining strength later in the year.
Marilyn Schaja of brokerage Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette generally agreed the expansion would struggle along, although she took the view that growth would be subpar, around 1 percent next year.
"The economy will continue to grow but at a very sluggish pace," she said.

The Conference Board report said five of the 10 indicators rose, four declined and one was unchanged. The largest increases were in stock prices, money supply, consumer expectations and building permits.
The declines included interest rate spread and manufacturers' new orders of non-defence capital goods and consumer goods and materials.
The report reflected changes made in calculating the index to refine its ability to forecast turning points in the economy. Two of its components were dropped and a new one was added.
In Monday's other report, the realtor group found evidence for some celebration as home resales in November seemed to put the industry back on a record-setting pace for this year.
"Consumer confidence is strong once again and this is resulting in heavy activity in markets coast to coast," said National Association of Realtors President Russell Booth.
The group anticipates existing-home sales will total 4.09 million units for the year, eclipsing the previous high of 3.99 million units recorded in 1978.
The activity is being helped by relatively benign interest rates.

The Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp reported the national average commitment rate of 30-year, conventional, fixed-rate mortgages fell to 7.62 percent in November from 7.92 percent in October, the group said.
The national median existing-home price was $117,400 in November, up 2.7 percent from November 1995 and compared with $116,600 in October.
The group projected a median price, the midpoint at which half the homes sell for more and half for less, at $117,700 for this year, an increase of 4.2 percent over 1995.
"The continued rise in the median price on a national and regional basis suggests that sales have remained steady in both first-time and trade-up markets," the realtor group said.
